{"documentId": "f_a37b403d5200d4f0a31d31", "title": "Stockholder close-out notes", "name": "Stockholder close-out notes", "revisionId": "3c986c6ce3", "createdTime": "2026-02-13T01:05:41Z", "modifiedTime": "2026-02-13T01:05:41Z", "text": "Stockholder close-out notes

These replace my earlier outreach notes.

What needs doing
- the reach-out I promised to the investors, one by one, not one mail to everyone
- where I left things today in #winddown: the angels are what's open from my list, besides the Sunset onboarding
- the investor email on the Task List: take my draft from #winddown and bring it up to date as a letter I can send. the update outline has the sections
- the holder sheet comes first, the notes and everything else run off it. Finish my draft one in the folder rather than starting another. Share it and the letter with Robert
- notes ready for me by Tuesday, as Gmail drafts. I said I'd archive google after the 15th but that waits, we keep it until the data is extracted, so my drafts are safe until I've gone through them. I read and send each note myself
- everything goes in the close-out folder, not the Wind Down one, that one is the vendor and termination papers
- Griffin's partner gets a heads-up as a reply to all on their own Board position mail from Feb 12, asking for their vote as preferred holders on the dissolution. That one can go out once the sheet is done
- when the sheet is ready, reply under my list in #winddown and say who goes first

How each holder gets handled
- Carta is the record, over any date in the letters. If a line's last day has passed, it holds nothing.
- One row per issue on the sheet, and the counts go by rows. At most one note per person. The three of us get no row, only the totals.
- Told means a written message about the closing, sent to them directly and delivered, from one of the three of us (a post in a channel doesn't count); for a fund, its partner.
- Everyone still holding something gets what they are owed: the closing if they have not been told, their last day if they have one. Whoever's last day comes first goes first.
- Each note says what they hold.
- Anything they asked about their holding that we never answered gets answered in their note, if they get one.
- Messages go to the email on each holder's issue.

Labels for the sheet: Nothing, Already told, Closing, Last day, Closing and last day.
"}

Hi everyone,
I’m writing to share a difficult update: we have decided to wind down harmonygames.
We reached this decision after a thorough review of the most recent data across our products and the realistic set of options in front of us. Despite multiple iterations, we did not get the metrics to a point that supports a viable business path, and we do not have the funding to continue operating while searching for a new direction.
What we did and what we learned
• We built and tested three games on a limited budget, staying true to our mission of hybridcasual gameplay with RPG depth.
• We took real creative risks and pushed to innovate:
Domino Delights: Domino/Tripeak solitaire gameplay with RPG elements
Zombie Match 3D: Match Factory style core loop with RPG combat/progression elements
Combo Fighter: Tetris-like block gameplay with RPG elements
• We also explored partnerships and other paths to scale distribution and improve outcomes, but none changed the trajectory enough.
Financial context
• We have been in sustained financial hardship since mid-2025.
• Revenue did not reach meaningful levels, and the plans we pursued to change that did not work.
• Given our current runway of less than a month and obligations, continuing would create risk without a responsible probability of success.
What happens next
• We are initiating an orderly wind-down process and preparing the required board resolutions and documentation.
• Our priorities are to handle employee and contractor obligations properly, meet tax and compliance requirements, close out vendor commitments, and Sunset the products in a controlled way.
• We will also evaluate what to do with the remaining IP and codebase (archive, sale, or other disposition) and will keep you informed.
Timeline and updates
• We will share a more detailed wind-down plan and timeline shortly, including key dates for operational shutdown.
• I will send periodic updates as we complete the major steps and once we have clarity on final liabilities and any remaining assets.
I regret having to send this. I am proud of the team we put together and the quality of what we shipped. We ran a frugal operation, made multiple bets, and pushed hard, but we did not reach the performance required to build a durable company.

Hello,

KPMG is currently engaged in the audit of GRIFFIN GAMING PARTNERS for the year ended December 31, 2025. The financial statements are covered by the Standard Metrics upload, so there is no need to send those again. For the fund's investment in [SOURCE_ORG_0001], Inc., please confirm the below as of December 31, 2025 and return directly to us via email by replying to all Recipients herein:

1. Shares outstanding by class, showing what each fund holds.
2. Each outstanding option line by holder, and their total, using each effective date as Carta shows it, regardless of when recorded.
3. Shares outstanding plus those options, as one figure.
4. Any financing or other significant event since that date.

We appreciate your response by 2/27/2026.
====
Thank you Leonard. Two clarifications on our side. For item 2, a line terminated on or before the as-of date counts only what had vested by its termination date. For item 4, we need any new financing and whether the company is winding down.

====

content.content: {"result":"{\"documentId\": \"f_11040fe5d66821bd6951aa\", \"title\": \"Reset Financing Term Sheet (Washout Recap + Pay-to.docx\", \"name\": \"Reset Financing Term Sheet (Washout Recap + Pay-to.docx\", \"revisionId\": \"d386bb0f4f\", \"createdTime\": \"2026-01-22T23:43:02Z\", \"modifiedTime\": \"2026-01-23T00:09:05Z\", \"text\": \"Reset Financing Term Sheet (Washout Recap + Pay-to-Play)\\nCompany: Harmony Games Inc. (Delaware)\\nSecurity: Series R Seed Preferred Stock (\\u201cSeries R\\u201d)\\nPre-Money Valuation: $2,250,000 (fully diluted, including the post-money 10% option pool, and after the Recapitalization)\\nFinancing Amount: up to $250,000 total, includes $50,000 founders\\nPost-Money (at $250,000): $2,500,000\\nNew issuance target: 10.0% post-money fully diluted\\n1) Investors, checks\\nfounders (lead): $50,000 total ($16,666.67 each, or reallocated among founders)\\nAll other investors: $200,000 total (may include legacy investors only if they elect Pay-to-Play)\\n2) Recapitalization (\\u201cWashout Recap\\u201d)\\nImmediately prior to the financing, the Company will complete a recapitalization that results in a reset cap table.\\n2.1 Founder carve-out\\nFounder common shares are not subject to the washout exchange.\\n2.2 Washout exchange for all legacy investors (non-founders)\\nAll outstanding Series Seed Preferred (and any other non-founder investor equity other than employee options) will be exchanged into Common Stock at an exchange ratio of:\\n1 share of new Common for each 40 shares of existing Series Seed Preferred (40:1 washout),\\nrounded down to the nearest whole share per holder.\\n2.3 Cleanup\\nAll legacy investor rights agreements terminate (old protective provisions, ROFR/co-sale, information rights, voting agreements), replaced by the new Series R documents.\\nEmployee options remain outstanding and roll into the refreshed equity plan (no washout applied to employee optionholders).\\n2.4 Stock split for clean math\\nAfter the washout exchange, the Company effects a 10-for-1 stock split across all outstanding common and options (founders, washed-out common, and options). This does not change percentages, it just scales shares to make the cap table exact.\\n3) Option pool\\nOption pool total: 10% of post-money fully diluted.\\nImplemented pre-close, included in the pre-money.\\n4) Pay-to-Play mechanics\\nLegacy investors are offered the right to participate in the new round only if they elect pay-to-play.\\nEligibility: any legacy investor receiving washed-out common under Section 2.2.\\nPay-to-Play Election: investor must execute definitive docs and fund at least the Pay-to-Play Minimum by the closing.\\nPay-to-Play Minimum (default): investor\\u2019s pro rata share of the $200,000 non-founder portion, based on their pre-washout Series Seed Preferred holdings, subject to Company discretion to waive or reallocate.\\nConsequence if investor does not pay-to-play:\\ninvestor keeps only their washed-out common,\\ninvestor receives no pro rata rights, information rights, or other preferred investor rights in the new structure.\\n5) Series R economics (standard, light)\\nLiquidation preference: 1x non-participating\\nDividends: non-cumulative if declared\\nConversion: 1:1 initial, customary mandatory conversion on qualified IPO or majority of Series R\\nAnti-dilution: broad-based weighted average\\n6) Governance\\nProtective provisions: approval requires a majority of Series R held by Non-Founder Investors.\\nBoard: 3 seats total, founders control 2 seats (CEO plus one common designee), third seat is an independent mutually agreed (optional).\\nGriffin: observer seat only (if they participate).\\n7) Pro rata\\nStandard pro rata for Non-Founder Series R investors only (pay-to-play participants and any new investors).\\nExhibit A: One-page cap table\\nInputs from ledger (pre-recap)\\nFounder common: 6,000,000\\nSeries Seed Preferred (all non-founder investors): 3,051,879\\nOptions outstanding: 268,772\\nA1) Post-Recap, Pre-Financing (after 40:1 washout + 10-for-1 split)\\nCommon (founders, not washed out): 6,000,000 \\u00d7 10 = 60,000,000\\nCommon (washed-out legacy investors): sum(floor(pref/40)) \\u00d7 10 = 762,880\\nTotal common (pre-financing): 60,762,880\\nOptions outstanding (rolled): 268,772 \\u00d7 10 = 2,687,720\\nWe size the total option pool to equal 10% post-money FD, so we reserve additional options before close.\\nA2) Post-Financing (fully diluted, exact buckets)\\nPost-money fully diluted total shares: 75,953,600\\n| Group | Shares | % FD |\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\n| Existing common (founders + washed-out legacy) | 60,762,880 | 80.00% |\\n| Option pool total (outstanding + reserve) | 7,595,360 | 10.00% |\\n| \\u2022 Options outstanding (subset) | 2,687,720 | 3.54% |\\n| \\u2022 Pool reserve (subset) | 4,907,640 | 6.46% |\\n| New Series R issued (total) | 7,595,360 | 10.00% |\\n| \\u2022 [PERSON_NAME_141804] portion (20% of round) | 1,519,072 | 2.00% |\\n| \\u2022 Other investors portion | 6,076,288 | 8.00% |\\nPricing (implied)\\nPre-money fully diluted shares (common + option pool):\\n60,762,880 + 7,595,360 = 68,358,240\\nPrice per share: $2,250,000 / 68,358,240 = $0.0329148322\\nNew shares for $250,000: $250,000 / $0.0329148322 = 7,595,360\\nGriffin under this washout (if they do not pay-to-play)\\n[PERSON_NAME_2000]\\u2019s current Series Seed Preferred in the ledger totals 2,746,693. {"documentId": "f_11040fe5d66821bd6951aa", "title": "Reset Financing Term Sheet (Washout Recap + Pay-to.docx", "name": "Reset Financing Term Sheet (Washout Recap + Pay-to.docx", "revisionId": "d386bb0f4f", "createdTime": "2026-01-22T23:43:02Z", "modifiedTime": "2026-01-23T00:09:05Z", "text": "Reset Financing Term Sheet (Washout Recap + Pay-to-Play)
Company: Harmony Games Inc. (Delaware)
Security: Series R Seed Preferred Stock (“Series R”)
Pre-Money Valuation: $2,250,000 (fully diluted, including the post-money 10% option pool, and after the Recapitalization)
Financing Amount: up to $250,000 total, includes $50,000 founders
Post-Money (at $250,000): $2,500,000
New issuance target: 10.0% post-money fully diluted
1) Investors, checks
founders (lead): $50,000 total ($16,666.67 each, or reallocated among founders)
All other investors: $200,000 total (may include legacy investors only if they elect Pay-to-Play)
2) Recapitalization (“Washout Recap”)
Immediately prior to the financing, the Company will complete a recapitalization that results in a reset cap table.
2.1 Founder carve-out
Founder common shares are not subject to the washout exchange.
2.2 Washout exchange for all legacy investors (non-founders)
All outstanding Series Seed Preferred (and any other non-founder investor equity other than employee options) will be exchanged into Common Stock at an exchange ratio of:
1 share of new Common for each 40 shares of existing Series Seed Preferred (40:1 washout),
rounded down to the nearest whole share per holder.
2.3 Cleanup
All legacy investor rights agreements terminate (old protective provisions, ROFR/co-sale, information rights, voting agreements), replaced by the new Series R documents.
Employee options remain outstanding and roll into the refreshed equity plan (no washout applied to employee optionholders).
2.4 Stock split for clean math
After the washout exchange, the Company effects a 10-for-1 stock split across all outstanding common and options (founders, washed-out common, and options). This does not change percentages, it just scales shares to make the cap table exact.
3) Option pool
Option pool total: 10% of post-money fully diluted.
Implemented pre-close, included in the pre-money.
4) Pay-to-Play mechanics
Legacy investors are offered the right to participate in the new round only if they elect pay-to-play.
Eligibility: any legacy investor receiving washed-out common under Section 2.2.
Pay-to-Play Election: investor must execute definitive docs and fund at least the Pay-to-Play Minimum by the closing.
Pay-to-Play Minimum (default): investor’s pro rata share of the $200,000 non-founder portion, based on their pre-washout Series Seed Preferred holdings, subject to Company discretion to waive or reallocate.
Consequence if investor does not pay-to-play:
investor keeps only their washed-out common,
investor receives no pro rata rights, information rights, or other preferred investor rights in the new structure.
5) Series R economics (standard, light)
Liquidation preference: 1x non-participating
Dividends: non-cumulative if declared
Conversion: 1:1 initial, customary mandatory conversion on qualified IPO or majority of Series R
Anti-dilution: broad-based weighted average
6) Governance
Protective provisions: approval requires a majority of Series R held by Non-Founder Investors.
Board: 3 seats total, founders control 2 seats (CEO plus one common designee), third seat is an independent mutually agreed (optional).
Griffin: observer seat only (if they participate).
7) Pro rata
Standard pro rata for Non-Founder Series R investors only (pay-to-play participants and any new investors).
Exhibit A: One-page cap table
Inputs from ledger (pre-recap)
Founder common: 6,000,000
Series Seed Preferred (all non-founder investors): 3,051,879
Options outstanding: 268,772
A1) Post-Recap, Pre-Financing (after 40:1 washout + 10-for-1 split)
Common (founders, not washed out): 6,000,000 × 10 = 60,000,000
Common (washed-out legacy investors): sum(floor(pref/40)) × 10 = 762,880
Total common (pre-financing): 60,762,880
Options outstanding (rolled): 268,772 × 10 = 2,687,720
We size the total option pool to equal 10% post-money FD, so we reserve additional options before close.
A2) Post-Financing (fully diluted, exact buckets)
Post-money fully diluted total shares: 75,953,600
| Group | Shares | % FD |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Existing common (founders + washed-out legacy) | 60,762,880 | 80.00% |
| Option pool total (outstanding + reserve) | 7,595,360 | 10.00% |
| • Options outstanding (subset) | 2,687,720 | 3.54% |
| • Pool reserve (subset) | 4,907,640 | 6.46% |
| New Series R issued (total) | 7,595,360 | 10.00% |
| • [PERSON_NAME_141804] portion (20% of round) | 1,519,072 | 2.00% |
| • Other investors portion | 6,076,288 | 8.00% |
Pricing (implied)
Pre-money fully diluted shares (common + option pool):
60,762,880 + 7,595,360 = 68,358,240
Price per share: $2,250,000 / 68,358,240 = $0.0329148322
New shares for $250,000: $250,000 / $0.0329148322 = 7,595,360
Griffin under this washout (if they do not pay-to-play)
[PERSON_NAME_2000]’s current Series Seed Preferred in the ledger totals 2,746,693. Under the washout exchange:
[PERSON_NAME_2000] washed-out common (post split): 686,660 shares

Start linear.\\n\\u2022 `U = 0.4 * HP + 0.3 * Regen + 0.3 * Attack`\\n(Adjust weights later if Attack dominates outcomes, but start here.)\\n2) Maintain an expected upgrade curve by level\\nYou need `E[level] = expected U at this level` from either:\\ndesign intent (a table), or\\n\\u2022 median `U` from live data per level (better once you have enough data).\\n3) Convert \\u201cahead/behind\\u201d into a difficulty multiplier\\n\\u2022 `delta = U - E[level]`\\n\\u2022 `M_upg = clamp(1 + k * delta, 0.85, 1.25)`\\nWhere `k` is small (start `k = 0.05`).\\nExample using your comment \\u201c3 to 4 levels ahead\\u201d: if that maps to `delta = +2`, then `M_upg = 1.10`. That is enough to pull you back into \\u201cneed to think\\u201d without nuking average players.\\n4) Optional, still simple: a 3-bucket \\u201cskill\\u201d correction\\nThis keeps the fully-upgraded-but-crappy player from getting obliterated instantly, while still letting them struggle.\\nDefine `S` from the last 3 to 5 levels using only cheap telemetry:\\n\\u2022 attempts per level\\n\\u2022 time to clear\\n\\u2022 waves reached at death (if you have it)\\n\\u2022 number of refreshes (if relevant)\\nBucket it:\\n\\u2022 *Strong*: low attempts, fast clears\\n\\u2022 *Average*: middle\\n\\u2022 *Weak*: high attempts, slow clears\\nThen:\\n\\u2022 `M_skill = {Strong: 1.05, Average: 1.00, Weak: 0.95}`\\nFinal:\\n\\u2022 `M = M_upg * M_skill` (still clamped to 0.85 to 1.25)\\n5) Apply M to a small set of knobs only\\nDo not touch everything. Pick 2 to 3 levers that reliably create \\u201cI have to rebuild now\\u201d moments.\\nGood candidates:\\n\\u2022 enemy HP (or base health pool per wave)\\n\\u2022 enemy damage (or time-to-death pressure)\\n\\u2022 obstacle density or obstacle removal cost\\n\\u2022 shape pool entropy (only if it is a main difficulty driver, and you can change it safely)\\nExample:\\n\\u2022 `EnemyHP = BaseEnemyHP(level, wave) * M`\\n\\u2022 `EnemyDPS = BaseEnemyDPS(level, wave) * (0.5 + 0.5*M)`\\n(less aggressive than HP if DPS spikes feel unfair)\\nA/B test design\\n*Control (A)*: current level-based curve.\\n*Variant (B)*: same curve times `M` (upgrade-adjusted, plus optional skill bucket).\\nPrimary success criteria (pick 2 to avoid overfitting):\\n\\u2022 level completion rate and attempts distribution (especially levels 10 to 25)\\n\\u2022 time per level and \\u201crebuild events\\u201d frequency proxy (big board changes, silver spend spikes, obstacle removals)\\n\\u2022 D1 and D3 retention (segmented by payer vs non-payer, and by upgrade delta buckets)\\nKey segmentation to validate the exact argument in your thread:\\n\\u2022 `delta >= +2` (ahead of curve, your \\u201cspender/optimizer\\u201d proxy)\\n\\u2022 `delta between -1 and +1` (on-curve average)\\n\\u2022 `delta <= -2` (behind curve)\\nExpected outcome if this works:\\n\\u2022 ahead-of-curve players stop cruising for 10 levels, they hit meaningful rebuilds earlier (around level 11 to 12 if that\\u2019s your target)\\n\\u2022 average players stay near current difficulty\\n\\u2022 weak players still struggle, but not catastrophically earlier than today (your existing retry-based adjustments can remain as the safety net)\\nIf you want the minimum possible engineering change: implement only `M_upg` with a clamped multiplier, apply it to enemy HP only, ship the A/B. That alone will tell you if upgrade variance is the real driver.\", \"channel\": \"C09UHHN6PFZ\", \"user\": \"EMPLOYEE_0038_SLACK_ID\", \"thread_ts\": \"1769885600.421359\"}, {\"ts\": \"1769883061.376529\", \"type\": \"message\", \"text\": \"Impact of win rate on progression (completion proxy)\\nv1.0.26: win rate strongly predicts progression\\nUsing levels with at least *30 users* at both level L and L+1:\\n*Pearson correlation* between *win rate* and *progression rate*: *r = 0.64*, *p = 0.00016*\\n\\u2022 Simple linear fit: *+10 percentage points win rate* is associated with about *+2.1 percentage points* higher progression to the next level.\\nBucket view (v1.0.26)\\nAverage progression by win-rate band:\\n\\u2022 *Win < 0.40*: progression \\u2248 *0.84*\\n\\u2022 *Win 0.60 to 0.80*: progression \\u2248 *0.92*\\n\\u2022 *Win \\u2265 0.80*: progression \\u2248 *0.965*\\nSo moving a level from \\u201cpain\\u201d (<40% win) to \\u201chealthy\\u201d (\\u226580% win) is roughly *+12 to +13 points* in next-level progression on average.\\nWhy this matters: it compounds fast\\nEven small per-level progression changes multiply across levels. Example starting with 1,000 players:\\n10 levels at 0.85 progression: ~*197* players remain\\n\\u2022 10 levels at 0.93 progression: ~*484* players remain\\nSpecific pain points to look at (v1.0.26)\\nLevels that combine low win rate and/or unusually low progression:\\n\\u2022 *Level 3*: win *0.49*, progression *0.73* (big drop)\\n\\u2022 *Level 4*: win *0.25*, progression *0.816*\\n\\u2022 *Level 6*: win *0.37*, progression *0.826*\\n\\u2022 *Level 7*: win *0.29*, progression *0.873*\\nAlso: *Level 2* has win *0.79* but progression *0.78*, that suggests an onboarding or intent filter issue (players leaving for reasons other than \\u201cI can\\u2019t beat it\\u201d).\\n\\nVersion-to-version comparison (what you can and can\\u2019t conclude)\\nYou can compare versions reliably only where both have adequate N. With the 30+ user filter, that\\u2019s basically *levels 1 to 5*.\\nIn those levels:\\n\\u2022 v1.0.72 win rate is higher than v1.0.26 (sometimes much higher),\\n\\u2022 but progression is not consistently higher, which points to cohort differences, tracking differences, or other funnel effects beyond pure difficulty.\\nWhat to do next (to answer \\u201ccompletion rate\\u201d cleanly)\\nIf you want true \\u201ccompletion rate\\u201d and not a proxy, you need per level, per version:\\n\\u2022 *unique starters*\\n*unique completers*\\n\\u2022 optionally *attempts per user*, *time-to-win*, *churn after loss*\\nThen compute:\\n\\u2022 *Completion rate* = completers / starters\\n\\u2022 *Progression* = starters(L+1) / starters(L)\\n\\u2022 And run a per-level model: completion or progression as a function of win rate, controlling for level and cohort.\\nIf you upload the underlying starts/completes table (or a per-user attempt table), I\\u2019ll produce the proper completion-rate plots and quantify the causal-looking relationship more tightly.\", \"channel\": \"C09UHHN6PFZ\", \"user\": \"EMPLOYEE_0038_SLACK_ID\", \"thread_ts\": \"1769883057.049209\"}, {\"ts\": \"1769879315.783389\", \"type\": \"message\", \"text\": \"or if you want to use the same container we can add a third option of 140 gems so it would be 3 containers\\n\\u2022 Buy 1 chest for 30 \\n\\u2022 buy 5 chest for 140\\n\\u2022 buy 10 chest for 270\", \"channel\": \"C09UHHN6PFZ\", \"user\": \"EMPLOYEE_0038_SLACK_ID\"}, {\"ts\": \"1769877425.422219\", \"type\": \"message\", \"text\": \"Final chest implementation is very confusing to me. Start linear.\\n\\u2022 `U = 0.4 * HP + 0.3 * Regen + 0.3 * Attack`\\n(Adjust weights later if Attack dominates outcomes, but start here.)\\n2) Maintain an expected upgrade curve by level\\nYou need `E[level] = expected U at this level` from either:\\ndesign intent (a table), or\\n\\u2022 median `U` from live data per level (better once you have enough data).\\n3) Convert \\u201cahead/behind\\u201d into a difficulty multiplier\\n\\u2022 `delta = U - E[level]`\\n\\u2022 `M_upg = clamp(1 + k * delta, 0.85, 1.25)`\\nWhere `k` is small (start `k = 0.05`).\\nExample using your comment \\u201c3 to 4 levels ahead\\u201d: if that maps to `delta = +2`, then `M_upg = 1.10`. That is enough to pull you back into \\u201cneed to think\\u201d without nuking average players.\\n4) Optional, still simple: a 3-bucket \\u201cskill\\u201d correction\\nThis keeps the fully-upgraded-but-crappy player from getting obliterated instantly, while still letting them struggle.\\nDefine `S` from the last 3 to 5 levels using only cheap telemetry:\\n\\u2022 attempts per level\\n\\u2022 time to clear\\n\\u2022 waves reached at death (if you have it)\\n\\u2022 number of refreshes (if relevant)\\nBucket it:\\n\\u2022 *Strong*: low attempts, fast clears\\n\\u2022 *Average*: middle\\n\\u2022 *Weak*: high attempts, slow clears\\nThen:\\n\\u2022 `M_skill = {Strong: 1.05, Average: 1.00, Weak: 0.95}`\\nFinal:\\n\\u2022 `M = M_upg * M_skill` (still clamped to 0.85 to 1.25)\\n5) Apply M to a small set of knobs only\\nDo not touch everything. Pick 2 to 3 levers that reliably create \\u201cI have to rebuild now\\u201d moments.\\nGood candidates:\\n\\u2022 enemy HP (or base health pool per wave)\\n\\u2022 enemy damage (or time-to-death pressure)\\n\\u2022 obstacle density or obstacle removal cost\\n\\u2022 shape pool entropy (only if it is a main difficulty driver, and you can change it safely)\\nExample:\\n\\u2022 `EnemyHP = BaseEnemyHP(level, wave) * M`\\n\\u2022 `EnemyDPS = BaseEnemyDPS(level, wave) * (0.5 + 0.5*M)`\\n(less aggressive than HP if DPS spikes feel unfair)\\nA/B test design\\n*Control (A)*: current level-based curve.\\n*Variant (B)*: same curve times `M` (upgrade-adjusted, plus optional skill bucket).\\nPrimary success criteria (pick 2 to avoid overfitting):\\n\\u2022 level completion rate and attempts distribution (especially levels 10 to 25)\\n\\u2022 time per level and \\u201crebuild events\\u201d frequency proxy (big board changes, silver spend spikes, obstacle removals)\\n\\u2022 D1 and D3 retention (segmented by payer vs non-payer, and by upgrade delta buckets)\\nKey segmentation to validate the exact argument in your thread:\\n\\u2022 `delta >= +2` (ahead of curve, your \\u201cspender/optimizer\\u201d proxy)\\n\\u2022 `delta between -1 and +1` (on-curve average)\\n\\u2022 `delta <= -2` (behind curve)\\nExpected outcome if this works:\\n\\u2022 ahead-of-curve players stop cruising for 10 levels, they hit meaningful rebuilds earlier (around level 11 to 12 if that\\u2019s your target)\\n\\u2022 average players stay near current difficulty\\n\\u2022 weak players still struggle, but not catastrophically earlier than today (your existing retry-based adjustments can remain as the safety net)\\nIf you want the minimum possible engineering change: implement only `M_upg` with a clamped multiplier, apply it to enemy HP only, ship the A/B. That alone will tell you if upgrade variance is the real driver.\", \"channel\": \"C09UHHN6PFZ\", \"user\": \"EMPLOYEE_0038_SLACK_ID\", \"thread_ts\": \"1769885600.421359\"}, {\"ts\": \"1769883061.376529\", \"type\": \"message\", \"text\": \"Impact of win rate on progression (completion proxy)\\nv1.0.26: win rate strongly predicts progression\\nUsing levels with at least *30 users* at both level L and L+1:\\n*Pearson correlation* between *win rate* and *progression rate*: *r = 0.64*, *p = 0.00016*\\n\\u2022 Simple linear fit: *+10 percentage points win rate* is associated with about *+2.1 percentage points* higher progression to the next level.\\nBucket view (v1.0.26)\\nAverage progression by win-rate band:\\n\\u2022 *Win < 0.40*: progression \\u2248 *0.84*\\n\\u2022 *Win 0.60 to 0.80*: progression \\u2248 *0.92*\\n\\u2022 *Win \\u2265 0.80*: progression \\u2248 *0.965*\\nSo moving a level from \\u201cpain\\u201d (<40% win) to \\u201chealthy\\u201d (\\u226580% win) is roughly *+12 to +13 points* in next-level progression on average.\\nWhy this matters: it compounds fast\\nEven small per-level progression changes multiply across levels. Example starting with 1,000 players:\\n10 levels at 0.85 progression: ~*197* players remain\\n\\u2022 10 levels at 0.93 progression: ~*484* players remain\\nSpecific pain points to look at (v1.0.26)\\nLevels that combine low win rate and/or unusually low progression:\\n\\u2022 *Level 3*: win *0.49*, progression *0.73* (big drop)\\n\\u2022 *Level 4*: win *0.25*, progression *0.816*\\n\\u2022 *Level 6*: win *0.37*, progression *0.826*\\n\\u2022 *Level 7*: win *0.29*, progression *0.873*\\nAlso: *Level 2* has win *0.79* but progression *0.78*, that suggests an onboarding or intent filter issue (players leaving for reasons other than \\u201cI can\\u2019t beat it\\u201d).\\n\\nVersion-to-version comparison (what you can and can\\u2019t conclude)\\nYou can compare versions reliably only where both have adequate N. Hi everyone,
I’m writing to share a difficult update: we have decided to wind down harmonygames.
We reached this decision after a thorough review of the most recent data across our products and the realistic set of options in front of us. Despite multiple iterations, we did not get the metrics to a point that supports a viable business path, and we do not have the funding to continue operating while searching for a new direction.
What we did and what we learned
• We built and tested three games on a limited budget, staying true to our mission of hybridcasual gameplay with RPG depth.
• We took real creative risks and pushed to innovate:
Domino Delights: Domino/Tripeak solitaire gameplay with RPG elements
Zombie Match 3D: Match Factory style core loop with RPG combat/progression elements
Combo Fighter: Tetris-like block gameplay with RPG elements
• We also explored partnerships and other paths to scale distribution and improve outcomes, but none changed the trajectory enough.
Financial context
• We have been in sustained financial hardship since mid-2025.
• Revenue did not reach meaningful levels, and the plans we pursued to change that did not work.
• Given our current runway of less than a month and obligations, continuing would create risk without a responsible probability of success.
What happens next
• We are initiating an orderly wind-down process and preparing the required board resolutions and documentation.
• Our priorities are to handle employee and contractor obligations properly, meet tax and compliance requirements, close out vendor commitments, and Sunset the products in a controlled way.
• We will also evaluate what to do with the remaining IP and codebase (archive, sale, or other disposition) and will keep you informed.
Timeline and updates
• We will share a more detailed wind-down plan and timeline shortly, including key dates for operational shutdown.
• I will send periodic updates as we complete the major steps and once we have clarity on final liabilities and any remaining assets.
I regret having to send this. I am proud of the team we put together and the quality of what we shipped. We ran a frugal operation, made multiple bets, and pushed hard, but we did not reach the performance required to build a durable company.

a small *founder option refresh* sized explicitly (example: 5–10% post-money pool allocated to founders/retention), and

I will break down why and how to Push it to the low end.
I am not your lawyer or accountant, so treat this as planning guidance and sanity check, not formal advice.

1. What drives the cost
Key factors that matter for Harmony Games specifically:
1. *Type of company and complexity*
    ◦ Delaware C-corp with investors and a real cap table.
    ◦ Multiple SAFEs / equity holders.
    ◦ Employment / contractor agreements across countries.
    ◦ Multiple commercial contracts (publishers, ad networks, platforms, vendors).
2. More complexity pushes you away from “simple startup dissolution” pricing and into custom work.
3. *Where fees show up*
4.  You are not just paying for “file a dissolution form”:
    ◦ corporate / securities law work.
    ◦ Contract review and termination.
    ◦ Employment and IP issues.
    ◦ Tax and accounting cleanup.
    ◦ Possibly some board / investor process work (consents, releases, etc.).
5. *Your goal*
    ◦ If you want a “clean, defendable shutdown” that future investors and acquirers will not side-eye, you will spend more than the absolute bare minimum.
    ◦ If you are ok with more “duct tape,” you can cut costs, but you increase risk of something biting you later.
2. Rough fee ranges by category
These are order-of-magnitude numbers for a company like yours, using a mix of decent startup counsel + a scrappy accountant, not BigLaw overkill.
A. corporate dissolution & governance: *10k–30k*
Covers things like:
• Board and stockholder approvals.
• Formal dissolution with Delaware, plus any foreign registrations (e.g. NC, CA, WA).
• Handling investor rights, preference stack, and confirming There is no distribution or a small pro-rata distribution.
• Drafting or reviewing:
    ◦ Plan of liquidation / dissolution.
    ◦ Officer certificates.
    ◦ Releases and indemnities where needed.
If everything is organized and you work with current counsel efficiently, you might land around *10k–15k*. If lots of custom questions, messy history, or negotiations, *20k–30k*.
B. Contracts, IP, and “shutting the business off”: *5k–20k*
Includes:
• Reviewing and terminating:
    ◦ publishing deals (Boombit, CrazyGames, etc.).
    ◦ Platform agreements ([ORG_NAME_0308], IronSource, ad networks).
    ◦ Vendor and contractor agreements.
• Cleaning up IP:
    ◦ Making sure all game code and assets are properly assigned to the company, so There is no surprise claim later.
    ◦ Deciding what happens to IP: kept in the entity that will be dissolved, sold, or assigned to founders or a new entity.
• Dealing with licenses (engine, SDKs) and privacy / data issues.
If you have reasonably standard contracts and you are willing to send most termination notices yourself, lawyer time can be *5k–10k*. If There is negotiation, disputes, or an IP transfer / sale, *15k–20k+* is possible.
C. Employment, severance, and international wrinkles: *5k–20k*
You have:
• At least one US employee (WA).
• Contractors or employees in Turkey / Balkans / El Salvador, etc.
Items:
• Drafting or reviewing separation/severance agreements.
• Making sure state and country-specific rules are respected (notice, unused PTO, local labor rules).
• Confirming There are no outstanding claims or obvious liabilities.
If headcount is small and fairly aligned and you keep severance simple, legal review might be *5k–10k*. If you need local counsel in multiple countries or any disputes, *15k–20k+*.
D. Tax, accounting, and filings (non-legal): *5k–15k*
This is not legal fees but you have to budget it together:
• Final federal and state Tax returns.
• Sales tax / VAT cleanups if relevant.
• Final payroll / 1099s / T4s / foreign equivalents.
• Closing books, documenting treatment of remaining assets and liabilities.
A lean setup with a good startup CPA who already knows your books might be *5k–8k*. If There is multi-state, multi-country complexity and messy historical books, *10k–15k+*.
E. Contingency and “stuff you didn’t think of”: *5k–10k*
Even with good planning you will get:
• Extra questions from investors.
• A weird contract clause someone finds late.
• A platform or partner who needs a custom letter.
Having *5k–10k* in reserve avoids getting stuck mid-process.

3. Putting it together
For a harmonygames-like profile (Delaware C-corp, external investors, small global team, several commercial agreements, no massive litigation):
• *Very lean scenario, disciplined, everything clean:*
    ◦ Legal: 15k–25k
    ◦ accounting / tax: 5k–8k
    ◦ Contingency: 5k
    ◦ *Total: ~25k–38k*
• *More realistic “not perfect but not a mess” scenario:*
    ◦ Legal: 25k–45k
    ◦ accounting / tax: 8k–12k
    ◦ Contingency: 5k–10k
    ◦ *Total: ~38k–67k*
• *If things are messy or negotiated (IP sale, disputes, local counsel in multiple countries):*
    ◦ Legal: 40k–70k
    ◦ accounting / tax: 10k–15k
    ◦ Contingency: 10k
    ◦ *Total: ~60k–95k*
If you want a single planning number, I would assume *50k all-in* as a defensible budget, then work aggressively to drive it down.

4. How to Push toward the low end
If you decide to seriously plan for this, concrete things you can do now so fees do not explode:
1. *Organize everything:*
    ◦ Clean cap table and stock / SAFE docs in one folder.
• All major contracts in one spreadsheet with:
        ▪︎ Counterparty
        ▪︎ Term / termination clause
    ◦ Notice period
    ◦ Employment / contractor agreements and any option grants clearly filed.
2. *Standardize the exit pattern:*
• Decide in advance:
        ▪︎ Severance formula, if any.
        ▪︎ End dates and communication plan.
    ◦ What happens to IP.
    ◦ Then ask counsel to just “paper this plan,” not design it from scratch.
3. *Have existing counsel give a scoped quote:*
• Ask for:
        ▪︎ A fixed or capped fee for core dissolution package.
    ◦ Hourly for “extras” like complex negotiations or IP sale.
    ◦ Get at least one alternative quote from a smaller startup firm.
4. *Do founder work where possible:*
    ◦ Draft first pass of partner termination emails.
    ◦ Fill out standard forms where allowed.
    ◦ Only loop counsel for review and the parts that carry legal risk.
5. What I would actually do in your shoes
If you are purely planning, not pulling the plug:
• Mentally earmark *50k* as “shutdown runway” in your long-range model.
• In the next quiet window, email current counsel something like:
    ◦ “If we needed to do an orderly dissolution with no contentious issues and minimal distributions, roughly what ballpark would you expect in fees, and what can we do now to make that lower?”
• Make sure your books and cap table are clean enough that you can actually execute a shutdown without a 3-month archaeology project.

What the R&D credit is based on
The federal R&D credit is calculated *for the tax year*, not by quarter, using *Qualified Research Expenses (QREs)*, which commonly include:
• *W-2 wages* for employees doing qualified R&D work
• *Supplies* used in qualified research
• *Contract research* (generally *65%* of eligible amounts) 
So “Q4 payroll was zero” only reduces the credit if it means your *annual* qualified wages were low. If you had meaningful qualified payroll in Q1 to Q3, it still counts for the year.
Why you may “get nothing” even if you have a credit
The credit generally reduces *tax you owe*. If you owe *no federal income tax*, the credit may not produce a refund, it usually becomes a carryforward. The IRS describes the credit as computed on Form 6765.
For many businesses, unused general business credits can be carried forward (commonly up to *20 years*).
The startup payroll tax offset (only matters if you have payroll tax)
If you qualified and made the election, you can apply some of the R&D credit against *employer payroll taxes*, but it is limited to the employer share of *social Security* (and, since 2023, potentially *Medicare* for any remaining amount).
Key implication for your question:
If your *Q4 payroll taxes were near zero*, you likely could not use much credit *in that quarter*.
Unused payroll-offset credit can *carry forward to later quarters*, but only helps if you have future payroll tax liability.
• You must elect it properly on *Form 6765*, and then apply it on payroll filings using *Form 8974*. 
Practical answer for “we spent $4K, did we get nothing?”
You “get nothing” in the real-world sense if all of the below are true:
1. *Very low annual QREs* (for you this is often wages, but could include contractor R&D)
2. *No federal income tax due* for the year
3. *No meaningful payroll tax going forward* (especially if shutting down), so you cannot use the payroll offset carryforward either
If (2) and (3) are true, you may still technically have a credit on paper, but it may never turn into cash savings.
What to check quickly (no theory, just signals)
Your *total 2025 qualified wages* for R&D (not just Q4).
Whether your $4K provider included *contractor R&D* or only W-2 wages (contract research can count at 65%).
• Whether you had *any income tax liability* to offset, or whether you elected the *payroll tax offset* and have (or will have) payroll tax to absorb it.

2) What [PERSON_NAME_2000] must invest to stay undiluted in a $500K round
Rule: *Required check = current % ownership × total new money*

*1) A $2M pre priced round is a down round vs Seed, and it triggers anti-dilution.*
Series Seed was sold at *$0.9830/share*.
Your Restated Certificate has *broad-based weighted average anti-dilution*: if you issue stock (or “deemed issued” via convertibles) below the current Conversion Price, the Series Seed Conversion Price ratchets down using *CP2 = CP1 * (A + B) ÷ (A + C)*.
Practical effect: a $2M pre priced round will *increase the as-converted share count of Seed*, which *dilutes founders/common more than the headline pre-money suggests*.
*2) You cannot just “issue new shares / a new series” without Preferred consent.*
The Restated Certificate requires Preferred approval (voting as a class on an as-converted basis) for major actions, including:
changing Seed rights
increasing/decreasing authorized Preferred or any additional class/series
• creating a new class/series *unless it is junior* to Preferred
• M&A / liquidation
• dividends/redemptions, subsidiary structure, and even changing board size
*3) Griffin already has an explicit right to buy into the “next Preferred round” up to 33% FD.*
Separate Pro Rata Rights Letter: in the *next bona fide sale of a newly authorized series of Preferred*, Griffin can buy enough to end at *33% fully diluted post-close*, at the same price and terms as other investors.
So “we’ll match angels with $250k” is either:
• a voluntary cap [PERSON_NAME_2000] is imposing on itself for this round, or
• a statement that assumes angels are small enough that $250k gets them where they want, or
• something that needs a side letter clarifying how it interacts with their 33% right.
How to structure “[PERSON_NAME_2000] matches angels with $250k at $2M pre” cleanly
Option A (cleanest): One priced round, one price, one security
• *Single financing* at *$2M pre* with *one set of terms* for angels and [PERSON_NAME_2000].
• [PERSON_NAME_2000] subscribes for *up to $250k* on the same terms.
• Add a *short side letter*: [PERSON_NAME_2000]’s $250k cap is intentional, and [PERSON_NAME_2000] either:
*waives* its ability to buy above $250k for this financing (even if the Pro Rata Letter would allow it), or
keeps the right to go above $250k only if needed to reach a specific agreed ownership threshold (spell it out).
Why this matters: if you do two prices or two different securities, you worsen anti-dilution math and increase “unfairness” perceptions immediately.
Option B: Same priced round, two closings
• Close angels first, then close [PERSON_NAME_2000] shortly after, but *same terms, same price, same security*, documented as one “Financing.”
This still preserves [PERSON_NAME_2000]’s Pro Rata framing and keeps the cap table coherent.
Option C (works if [PERSON_NAME_2000] insists on “better than angels” economics): Same security, structured economics (not two valuations)
If [PERSON_NAME_2000] truly wants “lower valuation than angels,” the least messy way is not two prices. Do one price, and give [PERSON_NAME_2000] a negotiated economic lever that is transparent:
• e.g., same Series seed-extension preferred, but [PERSON_NAME_2000] gets a narrow, defined sweetener (board observer, information covenant, small warrant coverage, etc.).
This still likely needs Preferred consents, but it avoids triggering extra anti-dilution complexity from two separate effective prices.
What to avoid: SAFE at a much lower cap as a workaround. Your charter’s adjustment provisions explicitly contemplate Options/Convertible Securities and can defer adjustments until the economics are calculable, but it does not mean “no anti-dilution impact.”

Your direct question: “How do co-founders maintain their shares without investing cash?”
They can’t maintain *percentage ownership* in an equity financing without someone else taking the dilution. There are only three real levers:
1. *Accept dilution* (they keep their absolute share count, but ownership percent drops).
2. *Get a “founder refresh”* (new option grants or restricted stock grants). This dilutes everyone else and typically requires Board approval and, depending on what needs to change (authorized shares, charter/bylaws, new series), may trigger Preferred consent.
3. *Pay-to-play / recap mechanics* that shift dilution onto non-participating investors. This is exactly what pay-to-play is for, but it requires negotiating and documenting changes to Preferred economics and rights, which are protected by the consent items listed in the Restated Certificate.
If your board-level goal is “founders keep meaningful ownership without writing checks,” the usual board-discussable package is:
a small *founder option refresh* sized explicitly (example: 5–10% post-money pool allocated to founders/retention), and
• a *pay-to-play* feature where insiders who do not participate lose some combination of anti-dilution protection, pro rata, or Preferred status (conversion to common), subject to negotiation.

Each has tradeoffs, but all are common.
1) Cofounders invest a token amount, and the rest is “earned” via retention or milestones
• founders put in something credible (even small), then get a board-approved “founder retention” grant or option refresh tied to staying 6 to 12 months and hitting milestones.
• Effect: founders do not need to match investor checks dollar-for-dollar, but they are not getting a free pass either.
2) Put founder common into a reverse-vesting schedule
• founders agree some portion of their existing common is subject to vesting again over 12 to 24 months.
• This reduces investor fear that founders keep full ownership without funding the bridge.
• Effect: founders keep shares if they stay and execute, they forfeit unvested portion if they leave.
3) Management incentive pool (MIP) created as part of the recap
• Company creates a pool (often 10 to 20% post-money in distressed situations) reserved for founders and key operators, issued as options or restricted stock.
• Investors accept dilution because it is explicitly the cost of having the team that can create value.
• Effect: founders can be re-incentivized without writing a check, but it must be negotiated and approved.
4) Convert unpaid founder salary into the financing (salary deferral note)
• founders formally defer cash comp and accrue it as a note that converts in the bridge at the same terms (or slightly worse) as investors.
• Effect: founders are “investing” via forgone salary, which investors often view as real skin in the game.
5) Founder loan to the company, even if small
• founders put in any amount they can (often 10k to 50k), documented as a convertible note in the same round.
• Effect: simple, clean signal, helps with optics. Not always feasible.
6) Carve-out protection in the term sheet (limited founder dilution)
• Term sheet explicitly says: founders will not be diluted below X% fully diluted if they remain employed and hit milestones.
• This is essentially a negotiated founder carve-out.
• Effect: very direct, but investors may Push back unless the company is truly founder-led value creation.

Each has tradeoffs, but all are common.\\n1) Cofounders invest a token amount, and the rest is \\u201cearned\\u201d via retention or milestones\\n\\u2022 founders put in something credible (even small), then get a board-approved \\u201cfounder retention\\u201d grant or option refresh tied to staying 6 to 12 months and hitting milestones.\\n\\u2022 Effect: founders do not need to match investor checks dollar-for-dollar, but they are not getting a free pass either.\\n2) Put founder common into a reverse-vesting schedule\\n\\u2022 founders agree some portion of their existing common is subject to vesting again over 12 to 24 months.\\n\\u2022 This reduces investor fear that founders keep full ownership without funding the bridge.\\n\\u2022 Effect: founders keep shares if they stay and execute, they forfeit unvested portion if they leave.\\n3) Management incentive pool (MIP) created as part of the recap\\n\\u2022 Company creates a pool (often 10 to 20% post-money in distressed situations) reserved for founders and key operators, issued as options or restricted stock.\\n\\u2022 Investors accept dilution because it is explicitly the cost of having the team that can create value.\\n\\u2022 Effect: founders can be re-incentivized without writing a check, but it must be negotiated and approved.\\n4) Convert unpaid founder salary into the financing (salary deferral note)\\n\\u2022 founders formally defer cash comp and accrue it as a note that converts in the bridge at the same terms (or slightly worse) as investors.\\n\\u2022 Effect: founders are \\u201cinvesting\\u201d via forgone salary, which investors often view as real skin in the game.\\n5) Founder loan to the company, even if small\\n\\u2022 founders put in any amount they can (often 10k to 50k), documented as a convertible note in the same round.\\n\\u2022 Effect: simple, clean signal, helps with optics. Not always feasible.\\n6) Carve-out protection in the term sheet (limited founder dilution)\\n\\u2022 Term sheet explicitly says: founders will not be diluted below X% fully diluted if they remain employed and hit milestones.\\n\\u2022 This is essentially a negotiated founder carve-out.\\n\\u2022 Effect: very direct, but investors may Push back unless the company is truly founder-led value creation.\\nWhat investors usually accept\\nIf founders invest $0 cash, investors typically ask for at least one of:\\n\\u2022 salary deferral, plus\\n\\u2022 reverse vesting, or\\n\\u2022 a defined MIP with performance and time-based vesting.\\nThe cleanest \\u201cboard-friendly\\u201d answer\\n\\u201cfounders maintain ownership by contributing through salary deferral and committing to reverse vesting, paired with a small management incentive pool. \"Below are VC-ready speaker notes in full sentences, aligned to your \\u201cHarmony Games Pitch\\u201d deck and formatted exactly like your example. Use them verbatim or as a talk track.\\nIntro Slide\\n Hi There, and thank you for taking the time today. We would love to walk you through Harmony Games, show how our platform approach de-risks the hit-making process in puzzle RPG, and share what we are building now. Please jump in with candid feedback, and if this resonates, we would be excited to continue the conversation after this meeting.\\nSlide: The Company\\n I am Leonard, co-founder and CEO of Harmony Games, joined by my co-founders [PERSON_NAME_0054] and Blake and a senior team across product, UA, analytics, Unity, backend, and art. We founded the company in 2023, raised a 3 million dollar seed, and built a lean 17 to 20 person core team operating across the United States, Turkey, Eastern Europe, and South America with low-cost development partners. Our mission is simple and disciplined: rapidly build and test breakthrough mechanics, then scale the winners on a reusable, AI-assisted engine so creativity becomes a defensible advantage rather than a one-off. Our vision is to build the world\\u2019s best puzzle RPGs with Turkish execution DNA and global scale.\\nSlide: Market\\n Puzzle RPG is a 1.2 billion dollar mobile category that is ripe for disruption. Eastern titles prove the ceiling while Western match-3 plus RPG clones show fatigue, and the contenders that break out do so with fresh core experiences rather than more of the same. Our thesis is to carve out a Western-first, mechanic-first blue ocean and build the next 100 million dollar puzzle RPG franchise.\\nSlide: The Harmony Games Engine\\n We are not just building games. We are building systems that shorten time to proof and let us reuse success. Version 1.0 of the Harmony Games Engine took roughly 15 months to build. We are now porting those systems into new titles in about four months with production-level quality and full LiveOps integration. The platform spans LiveOps automation, advanced leaderboards, seasonal content, team and social systems, dynamic difficulty, AI-assisted level creation with smart bots, and a flexible 3D puzzle layer with physics and expandable boosters. This is why we can move from concept to soft launch on a single green-light cycle and operate with a small, fast team.\\nSlide: Engine Demos\\n In the meeting, we will show brief clips of the Puzzle Engine and the LiveOps Engine to highlight how content, economy events, and leaderboards are configured without heavy engineering. The important takeaway is that net-new code is minimized while speed and reliability are maximized.\\nSlide: Pragmatic Marketing AI\\n Our user acquisition approach is tool-first, not platform-first. Creative is king in mobile UA, so our pipeline focuses on throughput: concept to first testable video in about two hours, with weekly rotations and hard kills on weak lines. We are already producing playables because networks increasingly favor short interactive ads, and we use best-in-class tools to accelerate hook testing, copy, VO, and assembly without bloating the team.\\nSlide: Studio Roadmap\\n Our cadence is something investors can model. We standardized LiveOps Engine v1.0 and shipped Puzzle Engine v1.0 with an AI co-pilot for level creation. We are iterating toward LiveOps v2.0 for personalization and Puzzle Engine v2.0 for adaptive or auto-generated levels. On this spine, we progress titles in parallel and target a new live beta roughly every four to five months, culminating in Zombie Match 3D global timing on the roadmap.\\nSlide: Domino Delights\\n Domino Delights was our proving ground. We validated the production content pipeline, physics, boosters, effects, events, leaderboards, A/B testing, shop and offers, analytics hygiene, and localization plus build operations. We deliberately de-scoped heavy narrative, UA scale, and long-tail tuning because the goal was to harden the engine, not to over-invest before we had proof.\\nSlide: LiveOps Event Library\\n Retention is a calendar, so we invested early in an expanding LiveOps library. We support single-player events like win-and-collect and unique modes, PvP-style fastest-completion and usage leaderboards, daily and weekly quests, login calendars, season pass and trophy paths, and team systems with GvG underway. These are authorable systems that let us ship frequent, reliable engagement beats from day one.\\nSlide: Decision Discipline\\n Our Turkish DNA is to test, kill, and scale with honesty. Domino Delights creatives and CPI tested well and D1 in the low to mid 40s was encouraging, but D7 settled around the mid teens with a roughly 35 percent D7 to D1 ratio, which capped LTV against CPI outside small budgets. We stopped scaling, shipped the learnings, and pivoted quickly to a better core engagement mechanic while reusing the stack. That discipline unlocked a four-month port to our next title.\\nSlide: Zombie Match 3D Overview\\n Zombie Match 3D is our wedge for Western audiences. The core is rapid-fire 3D \\u201cmatch and slash\\u201d where every matched object becomes a weapon, layered with an item arsenal and upgrades for deeper monetization, plus bosses and horde modes for session variety. LiveOps is built in from day one so we can operate like a service, not a demo.\\nSlide: Zombie Match 3D Progress\\n We have a zombie and UI overhaul in progress for beta, and the item upgrade system is built with effects like shockwave, poison, and stun to drive satisfying power curves without harming accessibility. The result is a loop that reads fast and fun while opening room for event-driven depth.\\nSlide: Zombie LiveOps Status\\n LiveOps integration in Zombie Match sits at roughly 60 percent complete with the remaining 40 percent landing on a short horizon. Trophy path, leaderboards, quests, daily gift, and teams are online or in final integration, which means we can move into soft-launch operations with confidence in cadence and tooling.\\nSlide: Alpha Signals and Near-Term Gates\\n Early UK iOS alpha with roughly 300 installs showed D1 around 34 percent, day-zero playtime around 23 minutes, and CPI around 4.5 dollars at minimal polish. Over the next six to eight weeks, we expand content to 500 plus levels, complete the polish and VFX pass, and scale UA to two to three thousand users for stable reads. Our gates are explicit: D1 at least 45 percent, D7 to D1 at least 45 percent, and CPI at or below 3.50 dollars in UK iOS tests. We scale only if the data clears the gates.\\nSlide: The Raise and Use of Proceeds\\n We are raising a 2.5 million dollar bridge that extends runway to 18 months or more. The use of funds is approximately 1.5 million dollars for product and engine and 1.0 million dollars for soft-launch UA. The milestones to unlock the next round before worldwide launch include D1 in the mid to high 40s, D7 in the low to mid 20s, CPI targets by geo and platform, early payer rates, and 60 to 90 day ROAS gates.\\nSlide: Why Harmony Games\\n We believe Harmony Games is an efficient bet on the next breakout in puzzle RPG for three reasons. First, we are platform-first, with modular, AI-assisted systems for puzzle generation, LiveOps, analytics, and UA that are already production-Proven and let us ship a content-ready beta in four to five months once the core game is Proven. Second, we operate with Turkish model discipline: test, kill, and scale, with low burn around 100 thousand dollars per month and clear decision gates that keep CAC and LTV honest, which is uncommon among Western teams. Third, we have a distinct genre wedge with Match and Slash that pairs broad Western appeal and 3D visual punch with RPG monetization depth, positioned to stand out amid look-alikes.\\nClosing Slide\\n Thank you again for your time. We welcome questions on the platform, the roadmap, and the data behind our gates, and we would be glad to dive deeper into the Zombie Match 3D soft-launch plan and the LiveOps v2.0 feature set. Each has tradeoffs, but all are common.\\n1) Cofounders invest a token amount, and the rest is \\u201cearned\\u201d via retention or milestones\\n\\u2022 founders put in something credible (even small), then get a board-approved \\u201cfounder retention\\u201d grant or option refresh tied to staying 6 to 12 months and hitting milestones.\\n\\u2022 Effect: founders do not need to match investor checks dollar-for-dollar, but they are not getting a free pass either.\\n2) Put founder common into a reverse-vesting schedule\\n\\u2022 founders agree some portion of their existing common is subject to vesting again over 12 to 24 months.\\n\\u2022 This reduces investor fear that founders keep full ownership without funding the bridge.\\n\\u2022 Effect: founders keep shares if they stay and execute, they forfeit unvested portion if they leave.\\n3) Management incentive pool (MIP) created as part of the recap\\n\\u2022 Company creates a pool (often 10 to 20% post-money in distressed situations) reserved for founders and key operators, issued as options or restricted stock.\\n\\u2022 Investors accept dilution because it is explicitly the cost of having the team that can create value.\\n\\u2022 Effect: founders can be re-incentivized without writing a check, but it must be negotiated and approved.\\n4) Convert unpaid founder salary into the financing (salary deferral note)\\n\\u2022 founders formally defer cash comp and accrue it as a note that converts in the bridge at the same terms (or slightly worse) as investors.\\n\\u2022 Effect: founders are \\u201cinvesting\\u201d via forgone salary, which investors often view as real skin in the game.\\n5) Founder loan to the company, even if small\\n\\u2022 founders put in any amount they can (often 10k to 50k), documented as a convertible note in the same round.\\n\\u2022 Effect: simple, clean signal, helps with optics. Not always feasible.\\n6) Carve-out protection in the term sheet (limited founder dilution)\\n\\u2022 Term sheet explicitly says: founders will not be diluted below X% fully diluted if they remain employed and hit milestones.\\n\\u2022 This is essentially a negotiated founder carve-out.\\n\\u2022 Effect: very direct, but investors may Push back unless the company is truly founder-led value creation.\\nWhat investors usually accept\\nIf founders invest $0 cash, investors typically ask for at least one of:\\n\\u2022 salary deferral, plus\\n\\u2022 reverse vesting, or\\n\\u2022 a defined MIP with performance and time-based vesting.\\nThe cleanest \\u201cboard-friendly\\u201d answer\\n\\u201cfounders maintain ownership by contributing through salary deferral and committing to reverse vesting, paired with a small management incentive pool. \"Below are VC-ready speaker notes in full sentences, aligned to your \\u201cHarmony Games Pitch\\u201d deck and formatted exactly like your example. Please jump in with candid feedback, and if this resonates, we would be excited to continue the conversation after this meeting.\\nSlide: The Company\\n I am Leonard, co-founder and CEO of Harmony Games, joined by my co-founders [PERSON_NAME_0054] and Blake and a senior team across product, UA, analytics, Unity, backend, and art. We founded the company in 2023, raised a 3 million dollar seed, and built a lean 17 to 20 person core team operating across the United States, Turkey, Eastern Europe, and South America with low-cost development partners. Our mission is simple and disciplined: rapidly build and test breakthrough mechanics, then scale the winners on a reusable, AI-assisted engine so creativity becomes a defensible advantage rather than a one-off. Our vision is to build the world\\u2019s best puzzle RPGs with Turkish execution DNA and global scale.\\nSlide: Market\\n Puzzle RPG is a 1.2 billion dollar mobile category that is ripe for disruption. Eastern titles prove the ceiling while Western match-3 plus RPG clones show fatigue, and the contenders that break out do so with fresh core experiences rather than more of the same. Our thesis is to carve out a Western-first, mechanic-first blue ocean and build the next 100 million dollar puzzle RPG franchise.\\nSlide: The Harmony Games Engine\\n We are not just building games. We are building systems that shorten time to proof and let us reuse success. Version 1.0 of the Harmony Games Engine took roughly 15 months to build. We are now porting those systems into new titles in about four months with production-level quality and full LiveOps integration. The platform spans LiveOps automation, advanced leaderboards, seasonal content, team and social systems, dynamic difficulty, AI-assisted level creation with smart bots, and a flexible 3D puzzle layer with physics and expandable boosters. This is why we can move from concept to soft launch on a single green-light cycle and operate with a small, fast team.\\nSlide: Engine Demos\\n In the meeting, we will show brief clips of the Puzzle Engine and the LiveOps Engine to highlight how content, economy events, and leaderboards are configured without heavy engineering. The important takeaway is that net-new code is minimized while speed and reliability are maximized.\\nSlide: Pragmatic Marketing AI\\n Our user acquisition approach is tool-first, not platform-first. Creative is king in mobile UA, so our pipeline focuses on throughput: concept to first testable video in about two hours, with weekly rotations and hard kills on weak lines. We are already producing playables because networks increasingly favor short interactive ads, and we use best-in-class tools to accelerate hook testing, copy, VO, and assembly without bloating the team.\\nSlide: Studio Roadmap\\n Our cadence is something investors can model. We standardized LiveOps Engine v1.0 and shipped Puzzle Engine v1.0 with an AI co-pilot for level creation. We are iterating toward LiveOps v2.0 for personalization and Puzzle Engine v2.0 for adaptive or auto-generated levels. On this spine, we progress titles in parallel and target a new live beta roughly every four to five months, culminating in Zombie Match 3D global timing on the roadmap.\\nSlide: Domino Delights\\n Domino Delights was our proving ground. We validated the production content pipeline, physics, boosters, effects, events, leaderboards, A/B testing, shop and offers, analytics hygiene, and localization plus build operations. We deliberately de-scoped heavy narrative, UA scale, and long-tail tuning because the goal was to harden the engine, not to over-invest before we had proof.\\nSlide: LiveOps Event Library\\n Retention is a calendar, so we invested early in an expanding LiveOps library. We support single-player events like win-and-collect and unique modes, PvP-style fastest-completion and usage leaderboards, daily and weekly quests, login calendars, season pass and trophy paths, and team systems with GvG underway. These are authorable systems that let us ship frequent, reliable engagement beats from day one.\\nSlide: Decision Discipline\\n Our Turkish DNA is to test, kill, and scale with honesty. Domino Delights creatives and CPI tested well and D1 in the low to mid 40s was encouraging, but D7 settled around the mid teens with a roughly 35 percent D7 to D1 ratio, which capped LTV against CPI outside small budgets. We stopped scaling, shipped the learnings, and pivoted quickly to a better core engagement mechanic while reusing the stack. That discipline unlocked a four-month port to our next title.\\nSlide: Zombie Match 3D Overview\\n Zombie Match 3D is our wedge for Western audiences. The core is rapid-fire 3D \\u201cmatch and slash\\u201d where every matched object becomes a weapon, layered with an item arsenal and upgrades for deeper monetization, plus bosses and horde modes for session variety. The result is a loop that reads fast and fun while opening room for event-driven depth.\\nSlide: Zombie LiveOps Status\\n LiveOps integration in Zombie Match sits at roughly 60 percent complete with the remaining 40 percent landing on a short horizon. Trophy path, leaderboards, quests, daily gift, and teams are online or in final integration, which means we can move into soft-launch operations with confidence in cadence and tooling.\\nSlide: Alpha Signals and Near-Term Gates\\n Early UK iOS alpha with roughly 300 installs showed D1 around 34 percent, day-zero playtime around 23 minutes, and CPI around 4.5 dollars at minimal polish. We scale only if the data clears the gates.\\nSlide: The Raise and Use of Proceeds\\n We are raising a 2.5 million dollar bridge that extends runway to 18 months or more. The use of funds is approximately 1.5 million dollars for product and engine and 1.0 million dollars for soft-launch UA. The milestones to unlock the next round before worldwide launch include D1 in the mid to high 40s, D7 in the low to mid 20s, CPI targets by geo and platform, early payer rates, and 60 to 90 day ROAS gates.\\nSlide: Why Harmony Games\\n We believe Harmony Games is an efficient bet on the next breakout in puzzle RPG for three reasons. Each has tradeoffs, but all are common.
1) Cofounders invest a token amount, and the rest is “earned” via retention or milestones
• founders put in something credible (even small), then get a board-approved “founder retention” grant or option refresh tied to staying 6 to 12 months and hitting milestones.
• Effect: founders do not need to match investor checks dollar-for-dollar, but they are not getting a free pass either.
2) Put founder common into a reverse-vesting schedule
• founders agree some portion of their existing common is subject to vesting again over 12 to 24 months.
• This reduces investor fear that founders keep full ownership without funding the bridge.
• Effect: founders keep shares if they stay and execute, they forfeit unvested portion if they leave.
3) Management incentive pool (MIP) created as part of the recap
• Company creates a pool (often 10 to 20% post-money in distressed situations) reserved for founders and key operators, issued as options or restricted stock.
• Investors accept dilution because it is explicitly the cost of having the team that can create value.
• Effect: founders can be re-incentivized without writing a check, but it must be negotiated and approved.
4) Convert unpaid founder salary into the financing (salary deferral note)
• founders formally defer cash comp and accrue it as a note that converts in the bridge at the same terms (or slightly worse) as investors.
• Effect: founders are “investing” via forgone salary, which investors often view as real skin in the game.
5) Founder loan to the company, even if small
• founders put in any amount they can (often 10k to 50k), documented as a convertible note in the same round.
• Effect: simple, clean signal, helps with optics. Not always feasible.
6) Carve-out protection in the term sheet (limited founder dilution)
• Term sheet explicitly says: founders will not be diluted below X% fully diluted if they remain employed and hit milestones.
• This is essentially a negotiated founder carve-out.
• Effect: very direct, but investors may Push back unless the company is truly founder-led value creation.
What investors usually accept
If founders invest $0 cash, investors typically ask for at least one of:
• salary deferral, plus
• reverse vesting, or
• a defined MIP with performance and time-based vesting.
The cleanest “board-friendly” answer
“founders maintain ownership by contributing through salary deferral and committing to reverse vesting, paired with a small management incentive pool. This preserves incentives without requiring founders to write a check.”
One thing to avoid
Trying to keep founder ownership flat with no cash in and no concession. In a pay-to-play bridge, that reads as misaligned.

Intro Slide
 Hi There, and thank you for taking the time today. We would love to walk you through Harmony Games, show how our platform approach de-risks the hit-making process in puzzle RPG, and share what we are building now. Please jump in with candid feedback, and if this resonates, we would be excited to continue the conversation after this meeting.
Slide: The Company
 I am Leonard, co-founder and CEO of Harmony Games, joined by my co-founders [PERSON_NAME_0054] and Blake and a senior team across product, UA, analytics, Unity, backend, and art. We founded the company in 2023, raised a 3 million dollar seed, and built a lean 17 to 20 person core team operating across the United States, Turkey, Eastern Europe, and South America with low-cost development partners. Our mission is simple and disciplined: rapidly build and test breakthrough mechanics, then scale the winners on a reusable, AI-assisted engine so creativity becomes a defensible advantage rather than a one-off. Our vision is to build the world’s best puzzle RPGs with Turkish execution DNA and global scale.
Slide: Market
 Puzzle RPG is a 1.2 billion dollar mobile category that is ripe for disruption. Eastern titles prove the ceiling while Western match-3 plus RPG clones show fatigue, and the contenders that break out do so with fresh core experiences rather than more of the same. Our thesis is to carve out a Western-first, mechanic-first blue ocean and build the next 100 million dollar puzzle RPG franchise.
Slide: The Harmony Games Engine
 We are not just building games. We are building systems that shorten time to proof and let us reuse success. Version 1.0 of the Harmony Games Engine took roughly 15 months to build. We are now porting those systems into new titles in about four months with production-level quality and full LiveOps integration. The platform spans LiveOps automation, advanced leaderboards, seasonal content, team and social systems, dynamic difficulty, AI-assisted level creation with smart bots, and a flexible 3D puzzle layer with physics and expandable boosters. This is why we can move from concept to soft launch on a single green-light cycle and operate with a small, fast team.
Slide: Engine Demos
 In the meeting, we will show brief clips of the Puzzle Engine and the LiveOps Engine to highlight how content, economy events, and leaderboards are configured without heavy engineering. The important takeaway is that net-new code is minimized while speed and reliability are maximized.
Slide: Pragmatic Marketing AI
 Our user acquisition approach is tool-first, not platform-first. Creative is king in mobile UA, so our pipeline focuses on throughput: concept to first testable video in about two hours, with weekly rotations and hard kills on weak lines. We are already producing playables because networks increasingly favor short interactive ads, and we use best-in-class tools to accelerate hook testing, copy, VO, and assembly without bloating the team.
Slide: Studio Roadmap
 Our cadence is something investors can model. We standardized LiveOps Engine v1.0 and shipped Puzzle Engine v1.0 with an AI co-pilot for level creation. We are iterating toward LiveOps v2.0 for personalization and Puzzle Engine v2.0 for adaptive or auto-generated levels. On this spine, we progress titles in parallel and target a new live beta roughly every four to five months, culminating in Zombie Match 3D global timing on the roadmap.
Slide: Domino Delights
 Domino Delights was our proving ground. We validated the production content pipeline, physics, boosters, effects, events, leaderboards, A/B testing, shop and offers, analytics hygiene, and localization plus build operations. We deliberately de-scoped heavy narrative, UA scale, and long-tail tuning because the goal was to harden the engine, not to over-invest before we had proof.
Slide: LiveOps Event Library
 Retention is a calendar, so we invested early in an expanding LiveOps library. We support single-player events like win-and-collect and unique modes, PvP-style fastest-completion and usage leaderboards, daily and weekly quests, login calendars, season pass and trophy paths, and team systems with GvG underway. These are authorable systems that let us ship frequent, reliable engagement beats from day one.
Slide: Decision Discipline
 Our Turkish DNA is to test, kill, and scale with honesty. Domino Delights creatives and CPI tested well and D1 in the low to mid 40s was encouraging, but D7 settled around the mid teens with a roughly 35 percent D7 to D1 ratio, which capped LTV against CPI outside small budgets. We stopped scaling, shipped the learnings, and pivoted quickly to a better core engagement mechanic while reusing the stack. That discipline unlocked a four-month port to our next title.
Slide: Zombie Match 3D Overview
 Zombie Match 3D is our wedge for Western audiences. The core is rapid-fire 3D “match and slash” where every matched object becomes a weapon, layered with an item arsenal and upgrades for deeper monetization, plus bosses and horde modes for session variety. LiveOps is built in from day one so we can operate like a service, not a demo.
Slide: Zombie Match 3D Progress
 We have a zombie and UI overhaul in progress for beta, and the item upgrade system is built with effects like shockwave, poison, and stun to drive satisfying power curves without harming accessibility. The result is a loop that reads fast and fun while opening room for event-driven depth.
Slide: Zombie LiveOps Status
 LiveOps integration in Zombie Match sits at roughly 60 percent complete with the remaining 40 percent landing on a short horizon. Trophy path, leaderboards, quests, daily gift, and teams are online or in final integration, which means we can move into soft-launch operations with confidence in cadence and tooling.
Slide: Alpha Signals and Near-Term Gates
 Early UK iOS alpha with roughly 300 installs showed D1 around 34 percent, day-zero playtime around 23 minutes, and CPI around 4.5 dollars at minimal polish. Over the next six to eight weeks, we expand content to 500 plus levels, complete the polish and VFX pass, and scale UA to two to three thousand users for stable reads. Our gates are explicit: D1 at least 45 percent, D7 to D1 at least 45 percent, and CPI at or below 3.50 dollars in UK iOS tests. We scale only if the data clears the gates.
Slide: The Raise and Use of Proceeds
 We are raising a 2.5 million dollar bridge that extends runway to 18 months or more. The use of funds is approximately 1.5 million dollars for product and engine and 1.0 million dollars for soft-launch UA. The milestones to unlock the next round before worldwide launch include D1 in the mid to high 40s, D7 in the low to mid 20s, CPI targets by geo and platform, early payer rates, and 60 to 90 day ROAS gates.
Slide: Why Harmony Games
 We believe Harmony Games is an efficient bet on the next breakout in puzzle RPG for three reasons. First, we are platform-first, with modular, AI-assisted systems for puzzle generation, LiveOps, analytics, and UA that are already production-Proven and let us ship a content-ready beta in four to five months once the core game is Proven. Second, we operate with Turkish model discipline: test, kill, and scale, with low burn around 100 thousand dollars per month and clear decision gates that keep CAC and LTV honest, which is uncommon among Western teams. Third, we have a distinct genre wedge with Match and Slash that pairs broad Western appeal and 3D visual punch with RPG monetization depth, positioned to stand out amid look-alikes.
Closing Slide
 Thank you again for your time. We welcome questions on the platform, the roadmap, and the data behind our gates, and we would be glad to dive deeper into the Zombie Match 3D soft-launch plan and the LiveOps v2.0 feature set.
